report:
# IBEX 35 Multifactor Screen — Executive Research Note

**Scope:** The six names below are this week's top-ranked constituents in a five-factor model (value 35% · quality 25% · momentum 15% · expectativas 15% · growth 10%). A rank position and a percentile score reflect relative standing *within the IBEX 35 today*, not absolute cheapness or quality, and not a recommendation. Percentile scores are also relative — they shift when peers move, independent of any change at the company itself.

Web search results for these tickers returned largely generic or unrelated content (e.g., IAG.MC search surfaced IAMGOLD, an unrelated Canadian gold miner; most other queries returned only quote-aggregator boilerplate). Where a genuine signal surfaced (BBVA's Q1 profit beat, Puig's referenced "record 2025" AGM statement, Logista analyst price targets), it is cited; otherwise commentary is confined strictly to the dataset provided.

---

### 1. IAG.MC — International Consolidated Airlines Group (Score 69.3, rank #1)

**What's carrying the score:** Growth (83.1) and expectativas (75.0) are the two strongest legs, with value (74.1) and quality (65.2) also above the index median. Momentum is flat at 50.0 — the price is not confirming the story (price is below both the 50-day and near the 200-day average, RSI neutral at 47).

**Does it hold up?** This is a broad-based score — four of five factors are solidly above median — but the flag here is explicit: **`beneficio_en_pico` is true**. Normalised profit growth of 72% and a normalised PER of 9.3x (vs. reported PER of 7.6x) sit on top of ROE of 42% and ROIC of 26.6%, which are extraordinary for an airline and almost certainly reflect a cyclical peak rather than a sustainable run-rate. Airlines are classic cyclicals where trailing and even multi-year "normalised" earnings can still be inflated near a demand peak — the "exceso_implicito_pp" of -63 (price implying *less* growth than history) looks attractive only if that history is representative, which peak-cycle earnings by definition are not. Leverage is also notable (debt/equity 160.7%, though net debt/EBITDA a manageable 0.74x and interest coverage 6.5x). Momentum's failure to confirm — price below its 50-day average despite the strong trailing 12-month return — is a legitimate tension with the rest of the score.

**Read:** A four-factor score, but resting on earnings that are explicitly flagged as being at a cycle peak. The value and growth readings should be treated as a snapshot of a good year, not a normalised run-rate.

---

### 2. MAP.MC — MAPFRE (Score 64.7, rank #2)

**What's carrying the score:** Expectativas is maxed out at 100.0 (the largest single contributor at 15% weight), with growth (63.3), value (63.6) and momentum (59.8) all moderately above median. Quality is the laggard at 48.4 — below the index midpoint.

**Does it hold up?** The expectativas score is doing a lot of work here, and the underlying number that produces it — exceso_implicito_pp of -63.8 — again says the market is pricing in far less growth than the trailing record shows. That's worth treating cautiously in an insurer, where reported profit growth (53.9% normalised) can be driven by non-recurring underwriting or investment-portfolio swings rather than durable operating improvement. The quality picture is mixed: ROE of 17.4% and ROIC of 8.1% are respectable but unremarkable, margins are thin (operating margin 5.15%), and FCF yield is negative (-10.2%) with negative FCF conversion (-1.17) — for an insurer, negative reported free cash flow needs the context of insurance cash-flow accounting (float, claims reserving) rather than being read as a distress signal, but it does mean the "value" score is not backed by a clean free-cash-flow story. **`beneficio_en_pico` is true** here too, reinforcing that the earnings base behind both the value and expectativas readings may be closer to a high-water mark than a sustainable average.

**Read:** A score built substantially on one factor (expectativas) plus a peak-earnings caveat on the growth and value legs. Quality is the visible weak point.

---

### 3. LOG.MC — Logista Holdings (Score 61.3, rank #3)

**What's carrying the score:** Quality is the standout at 75.0, with growth (61.6) and momentum (60.8) both above median and value more middling (51.7). Notably, **expectativas is entirely absent** from this company's factor set — it isn't scored (blank in the data), meaning the 61.3 composite is built from only four of the five weighted factors, with expectativas' 15% weight effectively redistributed or unfilled.

**Coverage flag:** **`cobertura_pct` is 75%**, the lowest of the six names here, and several inputs are explicitly null: FCF yield, FCF conversion, accruals ("devengos"), and exceso_implicito_pp are all missing. That means the value score (51.7) — despite Logista's very high headline ROE (42.5%) and ROIC (48.9%), strong interest coverage (51.4x) and net cash position (net debt/EBITDA -5.83x) — is not corroborated by any free-cash-flow read at all in this dataset. **`beneficio_en_pico` is true** as well.

**Read:** A quality- and momentum-led score with a full third-of-the-picture missing. Take the composite as directionally informative but not fully diagnosed — the absence of both a cash-flow check and an expectations check is a real gap given Logista's asset-light, low-margin distribution model (operating margin just 3.3%), where ROE/ROIC figures need cash-flow confirmation to be trusted.

---

### 4. BBVA.MC — Banco Bilbao Vizcaya Argentaria (Score 58.0, rank #4)

**What's carrying the score:** Momentum is overwhelming at 88.2 — the highest single-factor reading among all six names — driven by a 65% twelve-month return and price running 24% above its 200-day average. Growth (66.0) and value (59.7) are moderately supportive; quality (34.4) is the weakest reading in this entire group of six on that factor.

**Coverage flag:** **`cobertura_pct` is only 50%** — the lowest in the set. Debt/equity, FCF yield/conversion, deuda_neta_ebitda, EV/EBIT, ROIC, cobertura_intereses and margen_operativo are all null (expected for a bank under this generic template, since bank balance sheets don't map cleanly onto industrial leverage/FCF metrics — but it means half the intended diagnostic fields simply aren't available to corroborate the score). Reuters reporting cited in the search results does support a genuine fundamental datapoint: BBVA posted a 10.8% year-on-year increase in Q1 net profit, beating forecasts, with strength in Spain and Mexico — consistent with the momentum and growth readings, though that single data point doesn't validate the quality or value scores.

**Read:** This is essentially a one-factor score — momentum — riding on top of a growth reading that has some external corroboration, but with quality clearly lagging and half the data fields blank. The strong price action is real (confirmed independently), but the composite score's breadth should be discounted given the coverage gap.

---

### 5. PUIG.MC — Puig Brands (Score 57.7, rank #5)

**What's carrying the score:** This is the most evenly distributed profile of the six: quality 62.1, growth 62.7, value 57.6, momentum 54.9, and expectativas exactly at the midpoint, 50.0 — meaning the market's implied growth assumption is roughly in line with Puig's historical delivery, neither generous nor stingy.

**Does it hold up?** No factor is a standout and none is a serious laggard — this is a "many small positives" score rather than one built on a single lever. Fundamentals look coherent: FCF conversion of 0.86 (the strongest cash-conversion figure among value-relevant peers here besides Naturgy), moderate leverage (net debt/EBITDA 1.63x, interest coverage 14.3x), and a 17.5% operating margin. **`beneficio_en_pico` is true**, so the normalised PER of 19.65x and the growth/value scores still deserve the standard caution about extrapolating a peak year, but the AGM commentary referenced in search results (record 2025 financial performance) is at least directionally consistent with the profit growth shown here, rather than contradicting it. Cobertura is high at 94%.

**Read:** The most balanced, best-diagnosed profile of the group — broad, moderate contributions, good data coverage, no factor doing outsized work — but also the lowest-conviction "story" in the sense that nothing here is a strong positive signal either.

---

### 6. NTGY.MC — Naturgy Energy Group (Score 56.9, rank #6)

**What's carrying the score:** Value (67.2) and momentum (59.8) are the supports; quality (59.3) is middling. **Growth is the standout weakness at 10.9** — by far the lowest single-factor reading in this entire six-name set — driven by a -23.05% normalised revenue growth figure, even though normalised profit growth is still positive (8.74%). **Expectativas is not scored** (absent from the factor set), another gap in the picture, similar to Logista.

**Does it hold up?** The revenue contraction alongside profit growth suggests margin expansion or portfolio/scope changes (e.g., disposals) rather than organic strength — a pattern worth flagging rather than explaining away, since the data doesn't disclose the cause. Leverage is the highest debt/equity figure in the group after IAG (140.8%), though interest coverage (5.44x) and net debt/EBITDA (2.36x) are within a manageable utility-sector range. FCF yield (6.48%) and conversion (0.85) are solid. **`beneficio_en_pico` is true**, so the profit base behind the value multiple should again be treated as a possible high point rather than a trend.

**Read:** A value/momentum-led score dragged hard by growth, with the expectations check missing entirely. The revenue/profit divergence is the single fact here most in need of independent verification before drawing any conclusion about durability.

---

## Closing Ranking by Conviction

The screen's own score order is: IAG.MC (69.3) → MAP.MC (64.7) → LOG.MC (61.3) → BBVA.MC (58.0) → PUIG.MC (57.7) → NTGY.MC (56.9).

**Conviction-adjusted view** (i.e., how many independent, well-covered factors support each score, versus how much rests on one lever, a peak-earnings base, or a data gap):

1. **PUIG.MC** — Most balanced factor profile (no factor above 63 or below 50), highest data coverage (94%) among the non-financials, and an expectations reading that is neutral rather than stretched. The peak-earnings flag applies, but the AGM record-year reference at least doesn't contradict the trend. Lowest single-factor dependency of the six.
2. **IAG.MC** — Broadest positive score (four factors above median) and top of the ranking, but the entire value/growth/expectativas complex sits on explicitly peak, cyclical earnings, and momentum (the market's own verdict) is flat rather than confirming. Conviction is tempered relative to its score rank precisely because the story is strongest where the earnings base is most suspect.
3. **LOG.MC** — Strong quality and momentum readings, but a third of the relevant diagnostic fields (cash flow, accruals, expectations) are missing, and reported ROE/ROIC are unusually high for an asset-light distributor without a free-cash-flow figure to corroborate them. Peak-earnings flag applies.
4. **NTGY.MC** — Value and momentum support the score, but growth is the weakest reading across the entire group and stems from a revenue contraction alongside profit growth that the data doesn't explain — this divergence is the single largest unresolved flag in the set, and expectations aren't scored at all.
5. **MAP.MC** — The score leans heavily on one factor (expectativas at the maximum 100), quality is sub-median, and free cash flow is negative — a combination that inflates the perceived attractiveness of a name whose underlying operating quality is, by this data, the weakest leg of its own profile. Peak-earnings flag applies to the growth/value legs as well.
6. **BBVA.MC** — Momentum alone is doing almost all the work (88.2, the highest single reading among the six), quality is the group's second-lowest, and half of all data fields are missing. The one external data point found (a Q1 profit beat) supports the growth reading but does nothing to fill the quality/leverage gap. This is the case where the score order and conviction order diverge most: BBVA sits mid-table on score but arguably deserves the least weight given how narrow and thinly-verified its support is.

**Why the conviction order differs from the score order:** the score treats each factor as equally trustworthy once weighted; this note does not. Scores built on peak-cycle earnings (IAG, MAP, NTGY, PUIG all carry this flag), on a single dominant factor (BBVA's momentum, MAP's expectativas), or on incomplete data (BBVA at 50% coverage, LOG at 75%) are down-weighted in conviction even where the composite percentile is high. Puig's unglamorous, evenly-distributed, well-covered profile is the one case here where breadth and data quality — rather than any standout percentile — is the more persuasive feature.

*This note is research commentary derived from the factor data supplied and limited, largely inconclusive web search results. It does not constitute investment advice, and contains no buy, sell, hold or position-sizing recommendation.*

methodology.approach: Factor scoring, not threshold filtering. Every company in the index is ranked against every other on each metric, and the ranks are combined with the weights below. Nothing is rejected for scoring poorly — only for being impossible to evaluate.
methodology.why_not_filters: A hard filter chain (ROE > 20% AND P/E < 20 AND ...) discards a company at 19.8% ROE as readily as one at 3%, empties the screen when no name clears every bar, throws away how far each company cleared or missed, and silently gives RSI the same weight as ROE. A cross-sectional rank has none of those problems.
methodology.why_ranks_not_values: Scores are built from percentile ranks rather than raw values. One company emerging from a cyclical trough at +1,368% earnings growth would otherwise dominate any average and turn a multi-factor score into a single column in disguise. A rank treats that as what it is — first place — and nothing more.

value.what_it_measures: What you pay for what the business earns and owns. Built on normalised earnings rather than the last twelve months, so a company at the top of its cycle does not read as cheap.

quality.what_it_measures: Whether the business earns its returns on real capital and turns profit into cash. Accruals and leverage sit here because both are ways a good-looking profit can fail to be one.

momentum.what_it_measures: Whether the price agrees. Deliberately the lowest weight in the value screens: a company that has fallen is cheaper, not worse, and momentum should not be able to veto it.

expectativas.what_it_measures: How much growth today's price already demands, from the reverse DCF, against what the business has actually delivered. It is the only factor that scores the market's expectations rather than the company.

growth.what_it_measures: How fast revenue and earnings are compounding, measured against a multi-year base rather than a single prior year — a comparison against one weak year is arithmetic, not growth.

methodology.missing_data: A metric a company does not report scores nothing — never zero. Scoring a gap as the worst possible value punishes a company for a data provider's omission, and that is the kind of error that never appears in the table and decides the order anyway. A factor is averaged over the metrics that exist, and the weights are renormalised over the factors that exist.
methodology.coverage: Because weights renormalise, a company with thin data scores as confidently as a complete one. cobertura_pct is published alongside every score for exactly that reason: 90 on 40% coverage is an opinion about very little.
methodology.what_the_score_is_not: The score is a position within this index, not a grade and not a valuation. A company's score moves when other companies move. It says nothing about whether the name is worth owning, and it is not a recommendation.
methodology.read_the_breakdown: The per-factor scores matter more than the total. 'Cheap and high quality but no momentum' is a statement you can argue with; a composite of 67 is not.
methodology.two_stage: Four factors are ranked across the whole index (35 companies). The fifth, expectativas, comes from a reverse DCF that reads SEC filings and cannot run at that scale, so the top 12 are valued and ranked on it among themselves. The other four keep their index-wide percentile — re-ranking them inside an already-selected group would measure something different and read as if it did not.
methodology.report_size: The 6 highest-scoring companies go into the written report. That number is chosen rather than whatever a threshold happened to admit, which is what makes the cost of the run predictable.

valuation_method.model: Two-stage DCF on levered free cash flow (FCF discounted at cost of equity, compared with market cap — no net-debt bridge)
valuation_method.discount_rate: CAPM: currency-matched risk-free rate + beta x 5% ERP, beta clamped to [0.3, 2.5], rate clamped to [5%, 18%]. Only USD has a live quote (^TNX); other currencies use a documented static rate, flagged per company in risk_free_source.
valuation_method.implied_growth: Reverse DCF — the FCF growth rate that sets the model's equity value equal to today's market cap. What the price assumes, not a forecast. Available for every company, since it needs no history.
valuation_method.trend_test: A projection is only made when a least-squares line through log FCF reaches R2 >= 0.5. Below that the series is a path rather than a direction, dcf_value_per_share is null and dcf_skipped_reason says so.
valuation_method.probability: P(growth >= implied growth) under a Student-t fitted to the company's own year-on-year FCF growth in log space. Withheld entirely above a log stdev of 1.0, where it would be indistinguishable from a coin flip.
known_limits: History depth is uneven. SEC filings give US companies 14-17 years (16 growth observations for Adobe), but that source only covers SEC filers, so the IBEX screener and any company whose filing history has gaps falls back to yfinance's 4 years — 3 observations. Each company's fcf_source and probability.observations say which it got, and every probability is published as a range rather than a point.

A short FCF window can catch a trough, a spike or both and mistake it for a trend, and a long one can fit an earlier version of the company beautifully. The R2 test guards the first, and projecting the lower of the long-run and recent trends guards the second. Neither is a cure.
Terminal growth is a single 2.5% applied to every business regardless of its long-run ceiling; dcf_terminal_value_share_pct shows how much of each valuation rests on it.

The model sees free cash flow only — no revenue detail, margins, guidance or segments. A one-off legal settlement, licensing payment or deferred capex is indistinguishable from a genuine trend change, which is why revenue growth is carried alongside as a corroboration check.
Levered FCF is compared directly against market cap with no net-debt bridge — a deliberate simplification for data robustness across 500 tickers.

valuation_report:
# IBEX 35 Quality Screen — Reverse-DCF Reading

## 1. What each price is assuming

**IAG.MC (International Consolidated Airlines Group)** — The market is pricing in FCF *shrinking* at -6.24% a year in perpetuity terms. The cash-flow history (R²=0.83) does behave like a trend, and that trend has run at +56.7%/year, with revenue growth of only 12.9% — a 43.8pp divergence that suggests the FCF trend line is not simply revenue-driven. The implied growth sits 63 points below the trend growth (gap -63.0pp): the price is far more conservative than the airline's own recent cash-flow trajectory. No DCF value is published because the model's projectable growth (56.7%) falls outside the [-15%, 25%] band it's willing to extrapolate — the refusal is deliberate, not a data gap.

**LOG.MC (Logista)** — Implied growth is -11.89%, i.e. the price assumes ongoing FCF contraction. But R² is 0.419, below the 0.5 threshold, so the four-point FCF series (which includes a large negative year) does not behave like a trend at all — there is nothing reliable to compare the implied figure against. The DCF was skipped on trend grounds, not the growth-band boundary.

**AMS.MC (Amadeus IT Group)** — Implied growth is -4.75%, again a shrinkage assumption. Here the series is genuinely trend-like (R²=0.841), trend growth is +16.3%, nearly identical to historical CAGR (16.6%) and close to revenue growth (13.3%, divergence only 3.1pp) — three independent measures broadly agree. This is the one company where the model actually produced a DCF value (€318.58/share, +488% upside), but 82.7% of that value comes from the terminal 2.5% perpetuity, not the ten explicit years — the number is largely an artifact of one fixed long-run assumption, applied here as it would be to any other company on this list.

**PUIG.MC (Puig Brands)** — Implied growth of -6.48% versus a trend of +36.0% (R²=0.982, the tightest fit on the list). Historical CAGR (35.1%) and trend growth line up closely, but revenue growth is only 11.7% — a 24.3pp divergence, meaning the FCF trend has been running well ahead of revenue. Gap is -42.5pp: price assumes far slower growth than the recent trend. DCF was skipped because 36% growth sits outside the modelled band.

**MAP.MC (Mapfre)** — Implied growth -13.29%. R²=0.604 — just inside trend territory, but weakly so. Trend growth (+50.5%) and historical CAGR (+60.1%) both run far above revenue growth (+6.7%, divergence 43.8pp), a sizeable disagreement between FCF and revenue. Gap is -63.8pp, the widest on the list, but given the modest R² this should be read cautiously even though it clears the 0.5 bar. DCF skipped as growth falls outside the band.

**REP.MC (Repsol)** — Implied growth -3.06%, i.e. the price assumes mild shrinkage. The FCF series is trend-like (R²=0.855) but the trend itself is negative (-26.0%), roughly matching the historical CAGR (-27.8%) and directionally consistent with falling revenue (-10.0%, divergence -16.1pp). Here the gap runs the other way: +23.0pp — the price assumes a *less severe* decline than the recent trend implies, i.e. some built-in recovery expectation. DCF was skipped because -26% growth falls below the -15% floor of the modelled band.

**NTGY.MC (Naturgy)** — Implied growth -10.95%. R²=0.179 — no usable trend; the FCF path (2.56bn→2.43bn→1.80bn→2.38bn) does not describe a direction. Revenue fell 17.0% while FCF divergence is +11.9pp, but with no trend to anchor to, this is just a corroboration note, not a projection. DCF skipped for lack of trend.

**UNI.MC (Unicaja Banco)** — Implied growth is essentially flat (+0.34%), but trend_r2 is null — the four-year series swings from -17.4bn to +2.8bn to -0.4bn to -1.5bn (likely one-off items in a bank's cash-flow statement) and no trend fit was even attempted. Nothing can be said beyond the implied figure itself.

**BKT.MC (Bankinter)** — Implied growth -1.55%, again with no trend fit possible (series swings from -8.1bn to +1.8bn to -0.77bn). The model declined to project; the implied growth stands alone.

**AENA.MC (Aena)** — Implied growth is modestly positive at +2.05% — the only company on the list where the price assumes cash-flow *growth* rather than shrinkage. R²=0.493, just under the 0.5 threshold, so this is classified as non-trend-like even though it is close to the line; no gap was computed against it. Historical CAGR was 15.0%, revenue growth 14.5% (small 8.7pp divergence), but per the screen's own rule this cannot be treated as a reliable trend.

## 2. Trend-supported vs. model-declined

**Cash flows support a projection (R² ≥ 0.5):** IAG.MC, AMS.MC, PUIG.MC, MAP.MC, REP.MC. For these, the implied-vs-trend gap is a legitimate comparison (see above), even though only AMS.MC's growth fell inside the [-15%, 25%] band the model would actually extrapolate into a value — the others were still capped out by their own extreme trend growth (56.7%, 36.0%, 50.5%, -26.0%).

**Model declined to project (R² < 0.5 or no fit possible):** LOG.MC (R²=0.419), NTGY.MC (R²=0.179), AENA.MC (R²=0.493), UNI.MC (no fit), BKT.MC (no fit). For these five, the only defensible output is the implied growth figure itself, alongside the explicit reason no further comparison was made — that is the honest result, not a shortfall in the analysis.

## 3. Reading the probabilities

Every probability here rests on 3 (or fewer) year-on-year growth observations, so none should be read as a precise number — only the stated range:

- IAG.MC: 74.8%, range [67.8%, 87.6%]
- LOG.MC: 44.1%, range [31.9%, 46.5%] (only 2 observations)
- AMS.MC: 84.8%, range [77.2%, 94.5%]
- PUIG.MC: 96.6%, range [93.2%, 99.1%]
- MAP.MC: 73.5%, range [66.7%, 86.5%]
- NTGY.MC: 60.8%, range [57.3%, 70.2%]
- AENA.MC: 56.9%, range [54.6%, 63.4%]
- REP.MC: no usable estimate (1 observation)
- UNI.MC: no usable estimate (0 observations)
- BKT.MC: no usable estimate (1 observation)

A high band (PUIG.MC, AMS.MC) means that company's own historical growth cleared the implied bar in most of the (very few) years observed — it says the past was consistent with today's implied assumption being beaten, not that this will repeat. A wide range (IAG.MC, MAP.MC — both bands spanning roughly 13-20 points) reflects how little three data points can pin down. Where the probability is null, that is explicitly not a low probability — it is the model refusing to estimate one from an insufficient or contradictory sample.

## 4. Where this model is most likely to be wrong

- **Sample size.** Every probability is built on three year-on-year growth observations at most (often two, occasionally one). A Student-t fit on three points produces wide, unstable bands by construction; treat the range, not the point estimate, and treat even the range as approximate.
- **A four-year FCF window.** Four data points cannot distinguish a genuine structural trend from one phase of a cycle. IAG.MC (airlines), REP.MC (energy) and MAP.MC (insurance) are all cyclical or event-sensitive businesses; a four-year slice can easily capture a recovery leg or a trough and be read as a trend when it is really a phase.
- **A single 2.5% terminal growth rate for every business.** Where the DCF was actually computed (AMS.MC), 82.7% of the value comes from that one perpetuity assumption. The same 2.5% ceiling would be applied identically to a technology platform, a miner or a retailer, businesses with no reason to share the same long-run growth ceiling. This is the single largest driver of any DCF output on this list, more so than the ten years of explicit forecasting.
- **Cash flow with no context.** The model sees only the FCF number, never why it moved. IAG.MC's 43.8pp FCF/revenue divergence, MAP.MC's 43.8pp divergence, and PUIG.MC's 24.3pp divergence could reflect a genuine margin or working-capital shift, a one-off item, a legal settlement, a licensing payment, or a deferred capex program — the data here cannot distinguish between them, and no such claim is made.
- **Negative growth read as "cheap."** Where implied growth is negative (IAG.MC, LOG.MC, AMS.MC, PUIG.MC, MAP.MC, REP.MC, NTGY.MC, BKT.MC, and effectively UNI.MC), that is the market pricing in a shrinking business, not a discount to fair value — the two are not the same statement.

This is a description of what current prices assume and how that compares with each company's own recent cash-flow record — not an assessment of quality, value, or a recommendation to act on any name listed.
